slice: Deepening pass 3 for pre-2020 motocross models: magazine shootout verdicts, same-day dyno comparisons, used-bike guides with year-by-year weak points and fixes (knowledge push 2026-11)

records.statement: The 2011 450 SX-F was the first with rising-rate linkage rear suspension in place of the no-link system, in a smaller, slimmer package, at 242 lb. Known points: the radiator overflow could vent steam (cured with a longer vent hose routed under the cases), the nylon shock preload ring deforms and is hard to turn, and the spokes and rims need watching. Testers rated the handling and powerband highly.

source.name: Motocross Action - KTM 450SXF buyer's guide 2007 to 2020

records.statement: For 2012 the 450 SX-F got a diaphragm-spring (Belleville) clutch and a repositioned rear brake bleed hole. Tester fixes: the bars are too low (5 mm risers or bars 12-19 mm taller) and the gearing too tall (a 53-tooth rear sprocket was preferred). It is heavy for the class.

values.bar_fix: 5 mm risers or 12-19 mm taller bars

source.name: Motocross Action - KTM 450SXF buyer's guide 2007 to 2020

records.statement: The 2013 450 SX-F had a new engine and frame with fuel injection, plain bearings, a larger rear axle and a one-piece swingarm. It made 56.95 hp on a magazine dyno and weighed 240 lb, 3 lb less than 2012. Known points: the exhaust cannot come off without removing the shock (aftermarket systems with a separate mid-pipe avoid this), the seat foam is soft, and the stock suspension was criticised.

source.name: Motocross Action - KTM 450SXF buyer's guide 2007 to 2020

records.statement: For 2014 the 450 SX-F got a stiffer clutch spring, more fork compression damping and the 250 SX-F-style muffler. Known points: the rims are prone to loose spokes (stronger aftermarket rims were the cure), and the WP fork and shock fall short for heavier or faster riders, with a specialist fork rebuild suggested.

source.name: Motocross Action - KTM 450SXF buyer's guide 2007 to 2020

records.statement: For 2015 the 450 SX-F changed from the bladder fork to the WP 4CS, with new rims and tyres, axle and steering-stem changes and less weight. Known points: the air filter cage can unseat, the shock needed a stiffer spring (the 2014 spring was preferred), and if the fork is not using its travel, lowering the oil by 10 cc helps.

source.name: Motocross Action - KTM 450SXF buyer's guide 2007 to 2020

records.statement: The 2016 450 SX-F was 7.9 lb lighter than 2015 at 227 lb, made close to 58 hp, and gained rubber-mounted bars and a tool-free air filter. Known points: the fuel cap sticks, the fork dives and bottoms for faster riders, the brake pedal spring can pop off (turn it round and crimp the tangs), and the downsized rectifier can fail, with the 2015 or 2017 part used as the replacement.

source.name: Motocross Action - KTM 450SXF buyer's guide 2007 to 2020

records.statement: The 2017 450 SX-F got the WP AER 48 air fork and launch control and weighed 222 lb. Known points: sprocket bolts and spokes need constant checking (one test wheel broke five front spokes), neutral is hard to find at a standstill, the front brake hose can crimp, the fork clicker is small, the fuel cap sticks and the exhaust still cannot come off without removing the shock.

source.name: Motocross Action - KTM 450SXF buyer's guide 2007 to 2020

records.statement: The 2018 450 SX-F kept the AER fork and gained two-piece lower bar clamps and a push-button map and launch-control switch; it made almost 58 hp at 222 lb. Known points: the bar clamps can twist and deform their rubbers, the map switch is hard to use with gloves, the fuel pump relay hangs loosely, and the fork air valve is hard to reach with a cap that is easily lost.

source.name: Motocross Action - KTM 450SXF buyer's guide 2007 to 2020

records.statement: The 2019 450 SX-F made 57.13 hp stock and 58.12 hp with the airbox cover opened up; testers found the airbox choked at low rpm and opening the cover helped. It weighed 223 lb. Neutral is hard to find, the front brake hose can crimp, and older riders preferred the flex of the 2018 frame.

source.name: Motocross Action - KTM 450SXF buyer's guide 2007 to 2020

records.topic: CRF450R 2019 dyno, weight and price against the class
records.statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2019 CRF450R made 60.21 hp peak and 36.25 lb-ft at 7,500 rpm, with 37.52 hp at 6,000 rpm, 54.67 at 8,000 and 59.71 at 10,000, the most in the class. It weighed 238 lb without fuel and listed at $9,299.

source.name: Motocross Action - 450 motocross bike facts: horsepower, torque, price and weight

records.topic: FC 450 2019 dyno, weight and price against the class
records.statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2019 FC 450 made 56.40 hp peak and 35.31 lb-ft at 7,100 rpm, with 52.92 hp at 8,000 rpm and 55.46 at 10,000. It weighed 224 lb without fuel and listed at $9,999.

source.name: Motocross Action - 450 motocross bike facts: horsepower, torque, price and weight

records.topic: KX450 2019 dyno, weight and price against the class
records.statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2019 KX450 made 55.86 hp peak and 34.85 lb-ft at 8,500 rpm, with 37.68 hp at 6,000 rpm, 52.18 at 8,000 and 55.24 at 10,000. It weighed 233 lb without fuel.

source.name: Motocross Action - 450 motocross bike facts: horsepower, torque, price and weight

records.topic: 450 SX-F 2019 dyno, weight and price against the class
records.statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2019 450 SX-F made 57.14 hp peak and 35.79 lb-ft at 6,900 rpm, with 37.47 hp at 6,000 rpm, 53.92 at 8,000 and 55.85 at 10,000. It weighed 223 lb without fuel, the lightest in the class, and listed at $9,899.

source.name: Motocross Action - 450 motocross bike facts: horsepower, torque, price and weight

records.topic: YZ450F 2019 dyno, weight and price against the class
records.statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2019 YZ450F made 57.51 hp peak and 34.30 lb-ft at 6,900 rpm, with 57.18 hp still on tap at 10,000 rpm. It weighed 238 lb without fuel and listed at $9,299.

source.name: Motocross Action - 450 motocross bike facts: horsepower, torque, price and weight

records.topic: CRF450R 2016 dyno by rpm against the class
records.statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2016 CRF450R made 53.03 hp at 8,600 rpm and 33.63 lb-ft, the lowest of the six 450s on both counts: 35.66 hp at 6,000 rpm, 50.55 at 8,000 and 49.30 at 10,000. It peaks early and goes flat, and stays above 50 hp for only 1,900 rpm, the narrowest band in the class.

source.name: Motocross Action - how much horsepower do the 2016 450s make

records.topic: FC 450 2016 dyno by rpm against the class
records.statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2016 FC 450 made 57.14 hp at 9,600 rpm: 37.47 hp at 6,000 rpm, 53.54 at 8,000 and 56.32 at 10,000. It is strong everywhere and stays above 50 hp for 4,100 rpm, second only to the KTM.

source.name: Motocross Action - how much horsepower do the 2016 450s make

records.topic: KX450 2016 dyno by rpm against the class
records.statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2016 KX450F made 55.43 hp at 9,000 rpm, with 54.03 hp at 8,000 rpm and 51.55 at 10,000. The midrange is solid and the top end fades; it stays above 50 hp for 2,800 rpm, fifth of six.

source.name: Motocross Action - how much horsepower do the 2016 450s make

records.topic: 450 SX-F 2016 dyno by rpm against the class
records.statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2016 450 SX-F made 57.98 hp at 9,200 rpm and 36.63 lb-ft, the most of the six 450s on both counts: 38.63 hp at 6,000 rpm, 54.59 at 8,000 and 56.68 at 10,000. It stays above 50 hp from 7,200 to 11,500 rpm, the widest band in the class.

source.name: Motocross Action - how much horsepower do the 2016 450s make

records.topic: YZ450F 2016 dyno by rpm against the class
records.statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2016 YZ450F made 56.85 hp at 9,800 rpm: 37.27 hp at 6,000 rpm, 51.95 at 8,000 and 55.98 at 10,000. It has to be revved to reach its peak and is weaker than its rivals in the midrange; it stays above 50 hp for 3,800 rpm.

source.name: Motocross Action - how much horsepower do the 2016 450s make

records.topic: CRF250R 2016 dyno by rpm against the class
records.statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2016 CRF250R made 38.89 hp at 11,700 rpm: 29.96 hp at 8,000 rpm, 36.76 at 10,000 and 38.53 at 12,000. Low and mid power are strong and smooth, and it fades before the top.

records.topic: FC 250 2016 dyno by rpm against the class
records.statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2016 FC 250 made 44.38 hp at 13,900 rpm and 20.73 lb-ft, the highest peak in the class: 29.58 hp at 8,000 rpm, 36.60 at 10,000 and 44.23 at 12,000. It needs high rpm to make its power.

records.topic: KX250 2016 dyno by rpm against the class
records.statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2016 KX250F made 39.88 hp at 12,700 rpm and 20.05 lb-ft: 29.69 hp at 8,000 rpm, 36.47 at 10,000 and 39.61 at 12,000. Low-end response is crisp with good torque.

records.topic: 250 SX-F 2016 dyno by rpm against the class
records.statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2016 250 SX-F made 43.79 hp at 13,900 rpm and 20.20 lb-ft: 29.46 hp at 8,000 rpm, 36.49 at 10,000 and 43.79 at 12,000. It is a high-rpm engine that holds over 37 hp across a long band.

records.topic: YZ250F 2016 dyno by rpm against the class
records.statement: On a same-day magazine dyno the 2016 YZ250F made 39.35 hp at 12,000 rpm, with 35.53 hp at 10,000 rpm. It was the weakest of the six in the midrange on the dyno and gains strength near the top.

A magazine crew ranked the 2018 450 SX-F first of six 450s: the lightest (19 lb under the heaviest), with a long, usable powerband, the strongest brakes, a self-adjusting hydraulic clutch, accurate handling, precise shifting, air forks that work across rider weights and working launch and traction control. They listed no weaknesses.

A magazine crew ranked the 2018 FC 450 tied for second of six: 224 lb, with a smooth, metered powerband and a forgiving, accurate chassis. The clutch slave-cylinder seal was a reliability question. The baffled muffler is restrictive: the crew swapped it for the FC 250's, and riders wanting more punch can also drill the airbox.

A magazine crew ranked the 2018 CRF450R tied for second of six: a hard-hitting midrange, sharp turn-in, cleaner running on the new map and electric start, at 240 lb. Weak points: the seven-plate clutch with its judder spring breaks plates (replace the judder-spring set with an extra plate), slow-reacting brakes, forks that chatter over small bumps and dive on big hits, and no traction or launch control. The crew also ran stiffer springs, new mapping and a higher-pressure radiator cap.

A magazine crew ranked the 2018 YZ450F fourth of six: a single filled-in powerband, accurate turn-in, coil-spring forks, electric start and phone remapping, at 239 lb. It feels loose on corner exit and twitchy at speed and the stock map is weak. The crew ran a tuner-developed map, a 49-tooth rear sprocket and the lower bar mounts.

A magazine crew ranked the 2018 KX450F fifth of six: linear, usable low-to-mid power and predictable handling, but about 2.5 hp down on the leaders with no reason to rev past about 8,800 rpm. The clutch slips (stiffer springs), the chain guide wears fast (aftermarket guide), the air forks are dated and it benefits from new mapping.

A magazine crew ranked the 2017 450 SX-F first of six: 57.98 hp and 36.53 lb-ft, the broadest powerband, the best brakes and the best handling on the track. The shock spring had been lowered from 48 to 45 N/mm for 2017.

A magazine crew ranked the 2017 FC 450 second of six at 57.14 hp and 224 lb. The plastic airbox and restrictive muffler cost about 1.0-1.25 hp at every step from 5,000 to 11,000 rpm and add 2 lb: drill the airbox and fit a freer muffler. Their settings: 140-145 psi in the air fork for average riders and a 45 N/mm shock spring.

A magazine crew ranked the 2017 KX450F third of six: 55.43 hp, 35.79 lb-ft and 231 lb, with a smooth, linear powerband from the 2017 mapping and very good handling. The brakes are mushy from new (change the fluid early) and the clutch is only fair (stiffer springs or a complete aftermarket clutch).

A magazine crew ranked the all-new 2017 CRF450R fourth of six: 57.49 hp at 9,900 rpm and 233 lb, strong midrange drive and very good turn-in. Problems: jerky low-end mapping, a fork that is soft early then hits a firm shelf, a stiff clutch lever, a seat that unhooks on landings, radiators that pack with roost, and valves that went tight on the test bike. They wanted stiffer springs, better fork damping and a revised low-end map.

A magazine crew ranked the 2017 YZ450F fifth of six: 56.85 hp at 9,800 rpm and 238 lb, with excellent suspension and a strong top end. It is vague at the front and pushes in flat corners and the front brake is grabby. Their fixes: a 9-ounce flywheel weight, one tooth lower gearing, richer fuelling with retarded ignition, and for some testers 22 mm offset clamps in place of 25 mm.

A magazine crew ranked the 2016 450 SX-F first of six: the most power and torque, the lightest at 227 lb, the best shifting and brakes, at $9,299. The 4CS fork is valved for vets and novices, not pros, and the stock shock spring is too stiff for riders under 190 lb: revalve the fork and fit a 45 N/mm shock spring.

A magazine crew ranked the 2016 FC 450 second of six at 229 lb, with broad power and planted handling. The moulded airbox and muffler restrictor cost about 1-1.25 hp across the range and add 2 lb, and the 48 N/mm shock spring is too stiff for riders under 190 lb.

A magazine crew ranked the new 2016 KX450F third of six at 231 lb: much lighter, narrower and better handling than before, with air forks that work and a 270 mm front disc. It popped on deceleration and pinged late in motos, the clutch is marginal, shifting is mediocre and the brakes went spongy and needed bleeding.

A magazine crew ranked the 2016 YZ450F fourth of six at 238 lb, 11 lb more than the lightest bike: excellent suspension, a strong pull above 9,000 rpm and proven reliability, but vague at turn-in and inclined to push in flat corners, with a weak clutch. Their setup: a 49-tooth rear sprocket in place of the 48, the fork raised in the clamps and 103 mm of sag.

A magazine crew ranked the 2016 CRF450R fifth of six at 233 lb: lively off the bottom, tractable and predictable for local racers, with longer forks that calmed the front at speed. It has the least power and torque in the class, a spongy clutch, an air fork they rated poorly and a shock spring too soft for riders over 190 lb.

A magazine crew ranked the 2015 450 SX-F first of six: the broadest power, best brakes, hydraulic clutch, electric start and most accurate shifting. Its one weak point was the 4CS fork, which they sent out for a revalve.

A magazine crew ranked the 2015 FC 450 second of six. It shares the KTM engine but the restrictive airbox dulls throttle response; it has an easier low-to-mid transition, a resilient plastic subframe, a slippery seat cover, the same weak 4CS fork and a little more weight.

A magazine crew ranked the 2015 YZ450F third of six: the most power on the dyno by a clear margin, coil-spring suspension and very good durability. It is loud, the airbox fasteners pop off, the brakes are weak and it is uneasy on corner entry.

A magazine crew ranked the 2015 KX450F fourth of six: a strong, smooth powerband usable from novice to pro, mellowed for 2015, but with dated handling, a gearbox that resists shifting under load, a frail clutch and complicated triple-chamber air forks.

A magazine crew ranked the 2015 CRF450R last of six. It is light and nimble, but 2.5 hp behind the class leader at 8,000 rpm, 7.5 hp at 10,000 and 10 hp at 11,000, with a weak clutch, a tendency to flame out and twitchiness at high speed.

A magazine crew ranked the 2014 KX450F first of five on the strength of its engine: 55.05 hp at 9,000 rpm with the right power for every situation. Against that: quirky handling, weak brakes, a marginal clutch, a loud muffler, a weak chain guide and a big, bulky feel.

A magazine crew ranked the 2014 450 SX-F second of five: 56.95 hp at 9,400 rpm, usable power over the broadest range and the best brakes, clutch, shifting and handling. The WP suspension was average at best and the shock preload ring does not hold its setting.

A magazine crew ranked the new 2014 YZ450F third of five: 58.24 hp at 9,900 rpm, the most they had measured from a 450, with a seamless powerband, strong suspension and high durability. It is loose at the front on tip-in, lean on fuel and barks off the bottom: they richened the map, advanced the timing and changed the gearing.
A magazine crew ranked the 2014 CRF450R last of five: 51.97 hp at 8,600 rpm, the least in the test, with strong low-end and an easy, mellow feel but a narrow powerband that fades after 8,600 rpm.

A magazine crew ranked the 2018 250 SX-F first of six: 43.79 hp at 14,000 rpm, the lightest at 218 lb, $8,599, with the best top-end, clutch, brakes and balance. The stiff subframe makes the shock feel harsh, the 14/51 gearing is too tall for motocross (fit a 13-tooth countershaft) and only one of the three maps works well.

A magazine crew ranked the 2018 FC 250 second of six at 220 lb: strong top-end, plush air forks and a forgiving feel. The plastic airbox chokes low and mid power, the gearing is too tall and the stock map lacks bottom-end: drill the left airbox cover and fit a 13-tooth countershaft sprocket.

A magazine crew ranked the 2018 YZ250F third of six at 222 lb and $7,699: usable low and mid power, the best shock in the class and a planted rear in corners. The top end runs out early, turn-in takes effort, the brakes are weak and the airbox is loud. Their tips: raise the forks a few millimetres, short-shift, use the tuning tool, and a 51-tooth rear sprocket for slower riders.

A magazine crew ranked the new 2018 CRF250R fourth of six at 228 lb, the heaviest, and $7,999: excellent feel and forks, three maps and electric start, but almost no low-end torque, a narrow powerband that needs the clutch, tall gearing and an unbalanced stock chassis. Their fixes: lower the rear and raise the front, fit a 49-tooth rear sprocket (50 for slower riders) and re-map the third map with the tuning kit.

A magazine crew ranked the 2018 KX250F fifth of six at 221 lb and $7,749: smooth, easy power, a very adjustable chassis and excellent cornering. The stock map is too lean, the fork has a harsh spot mid-stroke, the shock setting is poor and the clutch wears quickly. Their fixes: remap with the tuning tool, a 51-tooth rear sprocket and the previous year's shock setting.

A magazine crew ranked the 2017 250 SX-F first of six: 43.79 hp, 218 lb, $8,499, with the most overall power and the lightest weight. The powerband demands full commitment and suits fast riders more than novices: resist shifting early, or stay in second gear until ready to rev it.

A magazine crew ranked the 2017 FC 250 second of six: 44.38 hp, the highest peak, 220 lb and $8,599, with smooth, broad delivery. The moulded plastic airbox dulls throttle response; drilling it is the fix.

A magazine crew ranked the 2017 YZ250F third of six: 40.98 hp, 222 lb, $7,699, with excellent suspension, a good clutch and strong low and mid power. The front brake is grabby, the handling middle-of-the-road and the airbox complicated.

A magazine crew ranked the 2017 KX250F fourth of six: 40.05 hp, 221 lb, $7,749, with very good handling, superb ergonomics and a broad, easy powerband. The forks, front brake, chain guide, shifting and clutch all need work; bleed the brakes after break-in.

A magazine crew ranked the 2017 CRF250R fifth of six: 38.89 hp, 224 lb, $7,599, light and nimble with good fork feel. It is low on power, the cable clutch is weak and it shakes its head when the setup is off. They advised against chasing power: matching the class leaders would cost about $4,000.

A magazine crew ranked the 2014 KX250F first of five: 41.14 hp at 12,200 rpm and the best engine in the class, broad and powerful. It understeers and stands up mid-corner, the gearbox is notchy and the brakes, clutch and durability are weak points.

A magazine crew ranked the all-new 2014 YZ250F second of five: 40.61 hp at 12,100 rpm and 221 lb, the lightest, with a strong midrange, coil-spring suspension and no reliability problems in testing. It hunts for traction, is vague at turn-in and has a weak front brake; race sag and fork height took time to get right.

A magazine crew ranked the 2014 250 SX-F fourth of five: 42.89 hp at 13,500 rpm, the most in the class, but 231 lb, the heaviest. It has a hydraulic clutch, the only electric starter in the class, excellent brakes and good reliability. The power is hard to use below the top end and the WP suspension is harsh.

A magazine crew ranked the 2014 CRF250R last of five: 37.25 hp at 11,200 rpm, the lowest in the class. It is easy to ride hard, comfortable, sharp-handling and light-feeling, which suits beginners and novices, but the suspension is too soft for anyone faster than a novice or heavier than 160 lb.

records.topic: CRF450R: which used year to buy (2017 against 2018)
records.statement: Magazine advice on used CRF450Rs: the 2017 is the better buy of the 2017-2018 pair. The 2017 weighs 233 lb and makes 57.49 hp but has no electric start. The 2018 added the starter and 7 lb with it, plus stiffer fork and shock springs and a revised map. A 2017 can be brought up to date with the dealer map update and a suspension shop setup, and 2018 head parts fit the 2017.

source.name: Motocross Action - looking for a used CRF450, but which one

records.statement: A magazine's used-bike advice steers buyers away from the 2009-2016 CRF450R generations and towards the 2017-on bike, calling the earlier ones flawed. Anyone riding one should weigh that against price and condition.

source.name: Motocross Action - looking for a used CRF450, but which one

records.topic: YZ450F 2014-2017: known problems and what to check
records.statement: Used-bike findings for the 2014-2017 YZ450F: the plastic free piston in the fork can crack and cause a loss of damping (anodised aluminium replacements exist, and the part was improved on later bikes); the sump plug and oil-filter cover bolts strip from over-tightening (thread inserts are the repair, and a weeping sump plug may mean damaged threads); the black plastic screen on the left of the engine can leak if over-tightened; a stiff rear end points to worn or seized linkage and swingarm bearings; and fuel line and pump connections leak if mishandled. Early bikes had aluminium lower engine mounts, later changed to steel.

source.name: ADB Magazine - used bike: 2014-2017 Yamaha YZ450F
